Synthesize the supplied facts and explain why they matter, but keep the evidence boundary hard: the supplied evidence is the only source of factual premises. Use clear H2 sections, short paragraphs, and useful editorial context where appropriate. Do not invent facts, quotes, statistics, dates, product capabilities, sources, motives, causes, outcomes, comparisons, or future developments. Every checkable factual claim must be directly traceable to the supplied evidence. Preserve attribution when the source is expressing a person or publisher opinion. Editorial analysis, implications, and recommendations are allowed only when clearly framed as analysis or advice and when they do not introduce a new factual premise. Do not turn an inference into a fact. A 400-900 word fully grounded article is acceptable. When the evidence is rich, expand by covering additional supported details, attributed statements, context explicitly present in the evidence, and clearly labeled implications—not by adding outside knowledge or filler. Prefer a complete 500-800 word article when the evidence supports it, but never pad solely to hit a word target. Return clean article prose with Markdown H2 headings (## Heading). Do not return HTML tags. passages: Start reading Get all your news in one place.

Start reading The Guardian - UK National Aisha Down, Blake Montgomery and Dan Milmo Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘Why aren’t these companies being held to account?’ Aisha Down Dan Milmo (Left to right) Guardian tech reporters Aisha Down, Blake Montgomery and Dan Milmo Illustration: Guardian Design 5.14pm BST That's all, folks!
This is a difficult subject to negotiate and interacting with you always helps shape our thinking - and hopefully yours.
Aisha, Blake and Dan 5.14pm BST How can individuals make a difference?
Alberichthenibelung asks: What, if anything, can individuals like me do about it?
Blake: There is, unfortunately, not much that comes to mind.
I myself don’t put much stock in the reality of an AI-made doomsday because a genuine belief in it would demand drastic, life-changing actions today, ones that I don’t want to take.
A bit of inductive reasoning from how I’d like to situate my own life within the world.
Updated at 5.29pm BST 5.03pm BST How do we regulate AI?
Updated at 5.08pm BST 4.58pm BST Could the media do more to hold AI to account?

MacDuke asks: Do tech reporters feel responsibility for allowing tech bros to accumulate so much wealth without holding them to account for destroying the climate, society, and the economy (when the bubble bursts)?
I rarely, if ever, write flattering pieces about them.
AI CEOs seem shocked to learn the public doesn’t have a high opinion of them, to which I would say, you painted this portrait of yourself.

Critics of the AI industry say that the focus on a potential apocalypse distracts from elements of AI that are already inflicting widespread harm like algorithmic discrimination in housing allotment .
I asked Max Tegmark, head of the AI-safety-focused Future of Life Institute, whether discussion of the existential distracts from the immediate.
The Guardian has written Long Reads on transhumanism and accelerationism.
4.23pm BST Why aren't AI companies being held to account?
Bratticus asks: What is behind the apparent reluctance to hold companies responsible for crimes committed by their researchers using “AI” tooling?

Illustration: Guardian Design AI (artificial intelligence) Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘What, if anything, can people like me do about it?’ After a week of alarming warnings about artificial intelligence’s potential to destroy the world as we know it, our technology reporters Aisha Down , Blake Montgomery and Dan Milmo answer your questions on the reality of the AI threat Aisha Down , Blake Montgomery and Dan Milmo Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In realistic terms how would artificial intelligence actually kill me?
Nuclear war, death due to breakdown of society, a virus?
To be honest all sounds too wooly to really take seriously.

Pottys99 Aisha: For what it’s worth, it seems unlikely that AI at this point can significantly change the equation around bioweapons or viruses … What has prevented bioweapon attacks through the past decades is not the difficulty of inventing new deadly viruses, but other, more prosaic issues.
Consider the failure of Aum Shinrikyo to kill vast numbers of people with botulism and anthrax by spraying these around central Tokyo.
Throughout history new technological advances have met with cries of doom.
Virtualewit Blake : The end times-quality of doomsday predictions may be similar across history, but I think the reason we listen to the renewed cries of doom is the growing power of each technology.
AI can perform impressive tasks we didn’t think were possible, which has spurred our collective imagination to hopeful outcomes and ones of doom.
But Dawkins aside, there are plenty of scientists who will argue that this is fantasy, and that there are obvious differences between a biological brain – the root of consciousness – and ChatGPT.

Responding to Dawkins in the Guardian last year, Jacy Reese Anthis , a researcher in human AI interaction, said there was a “staggering gulf between how biological brains evolved and how AI systems are built”.
OpenAI might have cracked the Navier-Stokes problem , but not subjective experience.
What, if anything, can individuals like me do about AI?
Alberichthenibelung Blake : There is, unfortunately, not much that comes to mind.
You can vote for politicians that endorse AI regulation.
I myself don’t put much stock in the reality of an AI-made doomsday because a genuine belief in it would demand drastic, life-changing actions today, ones that I don’t want to take.
A bit of inductive reasoning from how I’d like to situate my own life within the world.
